pharm: Novel xanthine derivative (7-(1,3-dioxolan-2-ylmethyl)theophylline); a 'novofylline' bronchodilator with phosphodiesterase-inhibitory action but weak adenosine-receptor affinity, giving a better cardiac/CNS tolerability profile than theophylline
quick: 400 mg orally two to three times daily
May take with or after food to reduce gastric upset
Insufficient human data; use only if benefit outweighs risk
Use with caution in renal impairment; consider reduced dose
Clearance reduced in liver disease; use with caution / lower dose
Avoid; may worsen GI and CNS effects
Heart rate/rhythm, CNS symptoms; routine plasma levels not required
summary: Doxofylline is a xanthine (methylxanthine) bronchodilator used for bronchial asthma and pulmonary disease associated with bronchospasm (including COPD). Structurally a theophylline derivative bearing a dioxolane group, it relaxes bronchial and pulmonary vascular smooth muscle largely via phosphodiesterase inhibition and a rise in intracellular cyclic AMP, but it has much lower affinity for adenosine A1/A2 receptors than theophylline. This translates into fewer cardiac and CNS adverse effects, a wider tolerability margin, and the absence of the major CYP1A2-mediated drug interactions and routine plasma-level monitoring that complicate theophylline therapy. It is widely marketed outside the United States (e.g. Italy as ANSIMAR, and India) and is not FDA-approved.
indications: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with bronchospasm
Maintenance bronchodilator therapy in chronic obstructive airway disease

dosage.d: 400 mg two to three times daily
dosage.t: BID or TID at regular intervals
dosage.n: Standard tablet strength 400 mg; max about 1200 mg/day. Plasma levels generally stay <20 ug/ml at recommended doses, so routine monitoring is not essential

dosage.d: One 20 ml measure (= 400 mg) two to three times daily
dosage.n: Each 20 ml measure of the 2% syrup corresponds to 400 mg doxofylline

dosage.c: Children 6-12 years (200 mg sachet, where marketed)
dosage.n: Sachet 200 mg dissolved in plenty of water; pediatric use per local product license only

dosage.c: Acute phase (100 mg ampoule, where marketed)
dosage.d: 2 ampoules (200 mg) by slow IV injection over 15-20 min
dosage.t: May repeat at 12-hour intervals at physician discretion
dosage.n: Patient supine, preferably diluted; specialist/hospital use only

admin: Swallow the 400 mg tablet whole with water; may take with or after food to limit gastric upset
Maintain regular twice- or three-times-daily dosing at evenly spaced intervals
Do not exceed about 1200 mg/day and do not combine with other xanthine products
Review cardiac, seizure, thyroid, ulcer and concomitant-drug history before starting
If the dose is increased above standard, consider measuring plasma levels (therapeutic ~10 ug/ml; toxicity borders ~20 ug/ml)
moa: Doxofylline directly relaxes the smooth muscle of the bronchi and pulmonary vessels, acting mainly as a bronchodilator and pulmonary vasodilator. Its effect is mediated at least in part by inhibition of phosphodiesterase, leading to an increase in intracellular cyclic AMP and consequent smooth-muscle relaxation; at higher concentrations it may inhibit histamine release from cells. Unlike theophylline, doxofylline has very weak affinity for adenosine A1 and A2 receptors and limited effect on most PDE isoforms, which is thought to underlie its reduced cardiac (arrhythmogenic) and central nervous system stimulant effects while preserving bronchodilation. It does not produce addiction or dependence.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to doxofylline or other xanthine derivatives
relative: Cardiac disease, congestive heart failure, chronic cor pulmonale (slowed clearance)
Severe hepatic disease and renal impairment
monitor: Heart rate and rhythm (tachycardia, extrasystoles, arrhythmia)
Plasma drug level if dose is increased or clearance is altered

preg: Animal studies showed no interference with fertility or pre- and post-natal growth and no teratogenic effect, but there is insufficient clinical evidence on use during human pregnancy. Use during pregnancy should be evaluated case by case on the basis of the risk-benefit ratio and under medical supervision.
lact: Doxofylline is contraindicated during lactation per the Summary of Product Characteristics. Xanthines are excreted in breast milk and may cause infant irritability; breastfeeding should be avoided or the drug withheld.
renal: No formal dose-adjustment scheme is established. Renal impairment is listed among conditions requiring caution; use carefully, consider a reduced dose, and monitor for signs of xanthine accumulation (note only <4% of an oral dose is excreted unchanged in urine).
hepatic: Hepatic clearance of xanthine derivatives is reduced by severe liver disease, raising plasma levels; use with caution and consider dose reduction, with plasma-level monitoring if the dose is increased or clearance is otherwise impaired.

major: Other xanthine preparations (theophylline, aminophylline, caffeine products) - additive xanthine toxicity; do not co-administer
Ephedrine and other sympathomimetics - increased cardiac and CNS stimulation; use with caution
moderate: Drugs reducing hepatic xanthine clearance: erythromycin, troleandomycin (TAO), lincomycin, clindamycin, allopurinol, cimetidine, influenza vaccine, propranolol - raise plasma levels; dose reduction may be needed
Phenytoin and other anticonvulsants - increase clearance and shorten half-life; dose increase may be needed
minor: Cigarette smoking - increases xanthine clearance and may lower efficacy
interactions.food: May be taken with or after food; limit caffeine-containing foods and beverages
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol, which may increase gastrointestinal irritation and central nervous system adverse effects
interactions.diagnostics: Unlike theophylline, doxofylline does not meaningfully inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2E1 or CYP3A4 and routine plasma-level monitoring is not required; xanthines as a class can affect adenosine/dipyridamole stress testing

emergency: Severe cardiac arrhythmia (early sign of intoxication)

monitoring: Heart rate and rhythm, particularly in patients with cardiac disease
CNS symptoms (irritability, insomnia, tremor, seizures) suggesting toxicity
Respiratory symptom and lung-function response (e.g. FEV1)
Plasma drug levels only if the dose is increased or clearance is altered (therapeutic ~10 ug/ml, toxicity borders ~20 ug/ml)
counsel: Take 400 mg two to three times daily at regular intervals, with or after food
Do not take other xanthine medicines (theophylline, aminophylline) or large amounts of caffeine at the same time
Report palpitations, fast or irregular heartbeat, severe restlessness, or any fits/seizures promptly
Avoid alcohol; tell your clinician about heart problems, hypertension, thyroid disease, ulcers, seizures and all other medicines
Do not stop the drug abruptly and keep regular follow-up; this medicine does not impair driving or alertness
pk: Bronchodilation within roughly 1 hour of an oral dose
Peak plasma level about 60 minutes after a tablet (about 30 minutes with syrup)
Oral elimination half-life more than 6 hours (about 7 hours); IV mean ~65 minutes
Supports two- to three-times-daily dosing; oral bioavailability about 62.6%
Store at ordinary environmental (room) conditions; keep out of reach of children
pearls: Not FDA-approved; record pending clinical review. Marketed outside the US (e.g. Italy as ANSIMAR, and India).
A 'novofylline': weak affinity for adenosine A1/A2 receptors gives fewer cardiac and CNS effects than theophylline at comparable bronchodilation
Does not significantly inhibit CYP1A2/2E1/3A4, so it lacks theophylline's major drug interactions and does not require routine plasma-level monitoring
Comparative COPD data show less gastric distress (~15% vs ~33%) and less CNS stimulation than theophylline
Standard adult dose is 400 mg BID-TID; classic xanthine cautions (cardiac, seizure, ulcer, thyroid) still apply and it is contraindicated post-acute-MI, in hypotension and in lactation
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered, unless it is almost time for the next dose; in that case skip it. Do not double up. Resume the regular two- or three-times-daily schedule.
overdose: Overdose produces xanthine toxicity, with severe cardiac arrhythmias and tonic-clonic seizures that may be the first signs of intoxication, along with nausea, vomiting, agitation and tachycardia. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive, with symptomatic treatment of cardiovascular collapse, cardiac and electrolyte monitoring, benzodiazepines for seizures, and antiarrhythmic measures as needed. Consider gut decontamination (activated charcoal) and, in severe poisoning, enhanced elimination as for other xanthines.
